q: Injurious immune reactions responsible for the pathology of many immunologic diseases
Types of antigens that can elicit hypersensitivity reactions
a: Exogenous (microbial or nonmicrobial: dust, pollen, food, drugs, chemicals) or endogenous (self antigens)

q: What hypersensitivity usually results from, in terms of immune balance
a: An imbalance between effector mechanisms of immune responses and the control mechanisms that limit them

q: The four major types of hypersensitivity reactions
a: Type I (IgE-mediated), Type II (antibody-mediated, cytotoxic), Type III (immune-complex mediated), Type IV (T-cell mediated, delayed type)

q: Hypersensitivity type triggered by binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on mast cells
Immediate reaction events in Type I hypersensitivity
a: Vasodilation, vascular leakage, smooth muscle spasm or glandular secretion; seen within minutes, subsides after a few hours

q: Late-phase reaction timing and features in Type I hypersensitivity
a: Seen 2 to 24 hours after exposure, up to several days; inflammatory cell infiltration (eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, monocytes, CD4 T cells) and tissue destruction

q: Mast cell mediator responsible for smooth muscle contraction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion
Mast cell lipid mediators that are vasoactive and spasmogenic

Example diseases from Type I hypersensitivity
a: Anaphylaxis, bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis/sinusitis (hay fever), food allergies

q: Cause of fall in blood pressure (shock) and airway obstruction in anaphylaxis
Hypersensitivity type in which antibodies react with antigens on cell surfaces or the extracellular matrix, causing cell destruction or interfering with function
Antibodies that may be involved in Type II hypersensitivity
a: Autoantibodies or antibodies against exogenous antigens bound to a cell surface/tissue matrix

q: Examples of Type II hypersensitivity reactions
a: Red blood cell destruction after mismatched blood transfusion; hemolytic disease of the newborn

q: Examples of Type III hypersensitivity diseases

Time frame for a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to become detectable

q: Type II hypersensitivity: antibody class, antigen form, and effector mechanism
a: IgG or IgM; cell-bound antigen; antibody binds cellular antigen, leading to complement activation and cell lysis (also ADCC)

q: Type III hypersensitivity: antibody class, antigen form, and effector mechanism
a: IgG and IgM; soluble antigen; antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissues, activate complement, and recruit neutrophils

q: Type IV hypersensitivity: mediating cells and mechanism
a: T cells; soluble or cell-bound antigen; TH1 cells secrete cytokines that activate macrophages and cytotoxic T cells

Mechanism where B cells expressing self antigens undergo antigen receptor gene rearrangement to acquire new, non-self-reactive receptors

How environmental triggers contribute to autoimmunity
a: Promote lymphocyte entry into tissues, activation of self-reactive lymphocytes, and tissue damage

q: General feature of autoimmune diseases regarding their course

q: What determines the clinical and pathologic manifestations of an autoimmune disease
